summary: First English narrative for FDA medical officer Frances Kelsey's 1961 decision to keep declaring Merrell's Kevadon (thalidomide) application incomplete, written from the case's verified facts (Kelsey's 'Autobiographical Reflections', FDA; FDA History pages).

narrative.hook: A sleeping pill used across Europe for years is waiting for your signature. The company says it is almost impossible to overdose on; you have just learned, from a medical journal and not from the company, that it can damage nerves. If you do nothing for sixty days, it is approved.
narrative.short_setup: It is spring 1961 at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Frances Kelsey, a physician and pharmacologist who joined the agency the previous August, has been reviewing the William S. Merrell Company's application to sell Kevadon, its brand of thalidomide, since early September 1960. The drug had been widely sold in Europe since about 1957 and was available in dozens of countries. Under the procedure then in force, an application became effective automatically sixty days after it arrived unless the FDA declared it incomplete and spelled out why. Kelsey, the chemist and the pharmacologist all found problems in the first submission, and Merrell has resubmitted. The company is pressing hard.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: The case for letting Kevadon through was not reckless. Thalidomide had years of wide use in Europe behind it. It was relatively non-toxic in animals, and its supporters pointed out that, unlike the barbiturates many people then took to sleep, it was very hard to take a fatal overdose. Merrell was willing to put warnings about nerve damage and about use in pregnancy on the label. Reviewers were expected to be fair to applicants, and an agency that kept blocking a drug used safely abroad, without any positive evidence that it caused harm, could fairly be accused of obstruction.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: The case for holding firm rested on the file itself. The clinical reports, about thirty of them, read more like testimonials than studies. The chemistry had still not been settled in January. And in late January or early February 1961 Kelsey had found, in a letter to the British Medical Journal, reports of peripheral neuritis, a painful and possibly irreversible nerve damage, in people taking the drug for long periods. Merrell's contact had seen that report and had not raised it. A sleeping pill that damaged nerves in adults raised an obvious further question: what might months of use do to a fetus? Merrell had no study of use throughout pregnancy. And a drug, once approved, was hard to pull back.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: Kelsey kept declaring the application incomplete. On 25 May 1961 Kelsey wrote to Merrell's contact man expressing concern that evidence of nerve toxicity had apparently been known to the company without being forthrightly disclosed. The FDA asked Merrell to question its American investigators about nerve damage, and asked what was known about use in pregnancy. In Kelsey's own later words, the objections were 'really on theoretical grounds, largely based on the fact that there was no evidence that it was safe'. In early September 1961 Merrell gathered its clinical investigators to make its case; by Kelsey's account, when the question of safety in pregnancy came up, it could not be answered.
narrative.outcome_story: The application never became effective. In late 1961 researchers in Germany and Australia linked thalidomide to clusters of rare and severe birth defects, eventually shown to involve thousands of babies. On 30 November 1961 Merrell told the FDA that the German maker was withdrawing the drug, and Merrell halted its American trials. Kevadon was never marketed in the United States. But Merrell had distributed more than two million tablets for 'investigational' use, a practice the law of the time left largely unchecked, and the FDA moved to recover them. According to Kelsey, Merrell formally withdrew its application on 8 March 1962. The near-disaster helped pass the Drug Amendments of 1962, which President Kennedy signed on 10 October 1962 and which required companies to prove drugs safe and effective before marketing. Kelsey received the President's Award for Distinguished Federal Civilian Service that year.
narrative.hindsight_analysis:
This is one of the most famous good decisions in public health, and that fame makes it harder to judge fairly.

On decision quality, the choice rates as strong, but for reasons that have little to do with birth defects. In spring 1961 nobody at the FDA suspected that thalidomide harmed babies. What Kelsey had were concrete problems in the application: weak clinical evidence, unsettled chemistry, and a serious side effect that came from the medical literature rather than from the company. The law allowed an incomplete application to be held, and approval was hard to reverse. The arguments for approval were real, the European record above all, but they did not fill those specific gaps. Kelsey later called the objections theoretical. That is the point: the decision was sound because it insisted on evidence, not because it foresaw the disaster.

On outcome quality, the result was good for the United States, where the drug never went on sale. It was not a clean escape. Millions of tablets had already gone out to doctors under loose rules for testing, and the FDA had to chase them down. And the good outcome depended on timing that no one controlled: the link to birth defects was made in Europe while the American application was still on hold. Had the European evidence come a year later, or the application been a cleaner one, the story could have ended differently.

The lesson is not that cautious regulators are always right. It is that 'no evidence of harm' and 'evidence of safety' are not the same thing, and that the burden of proof matters most when you cannot see what you do not know.
narrative.decision_principle: When the people asking for approval hold most of the information, absence of evidence of harm is not evidence of safety; insist on the evidence the decision actually needs, especially when the decision will be hard to reverse.
narrative.longform_story:
Frances Kelsey arrived at the Food and Drug Administration on 1 August 1960. Trained as a pharmacologist and a physician, Kelsey was one of only a handful of medical officers whose main job was to review applications from companies that wanted to sell new drugs. A few weeks later, in early September, Kelsey was handed one of the first: an application from the William S. Merrell Company of Cincinnati to sell a sleeping pill called Kevadon. Kelsey later recalled that the supervisors thought it would be an easy one for a newcomer. The drug was thalidomide, and it had been sold widely in Europe since about 1957.

The rules were simple and tilted toward the applicant. Once an application arrived, the FDA had sixty days. If it did nothing, the drug was automatically approved. To stop the clock, a reviewer had to declare the application incomplete and set out the deficiencies, and reviewers were expected to be fair about it. Any of the three reviewers, the chemist, the pharmacologist and the medical officer, could hold an application on their own.

All three found problems with Kevadon. The chemist, who could read German, found mistakes in the company's translations of the original German studies, and the chemistry was still not settled in January 1961. The pharmacologist raised a question about how well the drug was absorbed. Kelsey's own concern was the clinical evidence: some thirty doctors' reports that read more like testimonials than studies, backing claims Kelsey thought were far too glowing. The FDA told Merrell so. Merrell sent more information. The reviewers still found it wanting, and the company resubmitted.

In late January or early February 1961, browsing the British Medical Journal, Kelsey came across a letter published on 31 December 1960. It reported peripheral neuritis, a painful tingling of the hands and feet that could be severe and possibly irreversible, in patients who had taken thalidomide for some time. A mail delay had held up the journal. This did not seem the sort of side effect a simple sleeping pill should have. The FDA wrote to Merrell at once. When Kelsey raised it with Merrell's contact man, it emerged that the contact man had seen the report but had not mentioned it.

Merrell kept pushing. In April 1961 it argued for the drug by comparing its safety with the barbiturates, then the common sleeping pills; it was often said you could not kill yourself with thalidomide. Kelsey accepted there was something to that, but did not think it outweighed what was unknown. The company had hoped to sell the drug for the Christmas season of 1960, when sedatives sold well, and now a second Christmas was approaching.

This is the decision. On one side stood years of European experience, low toxicity in animals, a plausible safety advantage over barbiturates, the company's willingness to print warnings, and the duty to treat applicants fairly. On the other stood a thin and partly misleading file, a nerve side effect discovered in a journal rather than disclosed, and an obvious question no one had answered: if this drug could damage the nerves of adults over a few months, what might it do to a fetus exposed for nine? The FDA was already thinking about drugs and the unborn, after problems with other drugs in newborns. Merrell had no study of thalidomide used throughout pregnancy.

Kelsey kept saying no. On 25 May 1961 Kelsey wrote to Merrell's contact man about the apparent failure to disclose the nerve toxicity; Merrell's contact man thought the letter slightly libellous. The FDA asked Merrell to check with its American investigators for cases of nerve damage, and asked about pregnancy. Merrell would not run a pregnancy study but offered a warning on the label. In September the company brought its clinical investigators together to argue its case. By Kelsey's account, when the question of whether thalidomide was safe in pregnancy came up, the criticism of the FDA ended, because it was clear the data were not there.

Then, in the last weeks of 1961, the news came from Europe. Doctors in Germany and Australia had connected thalidomide to a wave of rare and terrible birth defects, babies born with severely shortened or missing limbs. On 30 November Merrell called the FDA to say the German maker was withdrawing the drug. Kelsey later admitted being very surprised. The FDA's objections, Kelsey wrote, had been 'really on theoretical grounds, largely based on the fact that there was no evidence that it was safe'.

Kevadon was never sold in the United States. But the escape was not complete. Under the loose rules for drug testing, Merrell had handed out more than two million tablets to doctors for 'investigational' use, far beyond the thirty or forty investigators named in the application, and the FDA had to launch a campaign to recover them. Merrell formally withdrew the application on 8 March 1962, according to Kelsey. That October, President Kennedy signed the Drug Amendments of 1962, requiring companies to prove that drugs were safe and effective before marketing them, and tightening the rules on clinical trials. Kelsey received the President's Award for Distinguished Federal Civilian Service.

It is tempting to tell this as a story of a reviewer who sensed a catastrophe coming. Kelsey's own account does not support that. No one at the FDA suspected birth defects in 1961. What Kelsey did was simpler and more useful as a lesson: refuse to treat the absence of evidence of harm as evidence of safety, insist that the company prove its case, and take seriously a warning sign that the company had not volunteered. The disaster that followed in Europe showed how much that mattered. But the decision would have been sound even if thalidomide had turned out to be harmless.
